subject: Chemistry
title: Avogadro's Number: Counting Atoms
description: A 60-second lesson on Avogadro's Number: Counting Atoms.

hook.text: One mole of any substance contains exactly 602,214,076,000,000,000,000,000 particles. That's Avogadro's number.

buildup.text: In 1811, Avogadro proposed that equal volumes of gas at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of particles.

discovery.text: This meant you could count atoms by weighing them. One mole of carbon weighs 12 grams and contains 6.022 × 10²³ atoms.

twist.text: Avogadro never knew his number. It was calculated 50 years after his death by Johann Loschmidt.

climax.text: If you counted one atom per second, it would take 19 quadrillion years to count one mole. That's a big number.

punchline.text: A bridge between the atomic and human scale. Weigh to count.

details.summary: Avogadro's number, approximately 6.022 times ten to the twenty-third, defines how many particles are in one mole of any substance. Amedeo Avogadro hypothesized in 1811 that equal volumes of gases at the same conditions contain equal numbers of molecules.
details.whyItMatters: Avogadro's number bridges the atomic and macroscopic worlds. Without it, chemists could not convert between measurable grams and the invisible particles that actually participate in reactions.
takeaways: One mole of any substance contains 6.022 times 10^23 particles
Avogadro proposed equal gas volumes hold equal molecule counts
His hypothesis was ignored for decades until Cannizzaro revived it

faq.question: How was Avogadro's number actually measured?
faq.answer: Multiple methods have been used, including measuring Brownian motion, X-ray crystallography of silicon spheres, and electrical charge experiments. Jean Perrin earned the 1926 Nobel Prize for experimentally determining the number through Brownian motion observations.

faq.question: Why was Avogadro's hypothesis ignored for fifty years?
faq.answer: Scientists confused atoms and molecules, and Dalton's framework did not accommodate diatomic elements. It took Stanislao Cannizzaro's systematic clarification at the 1860 Karlsruhe Congress to demonstrate how Avogadro's hypothesis resolved contradictions in atomic weight measurements.
